newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK- Wild talk, but little action.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK- Wild talk, but little action.

text.p: The final week of an extraordinary session of Brazil's Congress, called to run through the July recess, started with a bang but looks set to go out with a whimper.
Although no important votes were scheduled, government whips already had their hands full trying to limit the fallout from a latest outburst by controversial Communications Minister Sergio Motta.

In an interview published in magazine Veja Sunday, Motta said he was "disappointed" that recent cabinet appointments of two members of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) had not led to more support from the party for the government.
Another PMDB-sponsored appointment of the son of a construction company executive to run the highway department of Minas Gerais state was "shameful," Motta told Veja.

The minister also criticized the performance of the head of Brazil's state-run postal service who was nominated to the post by another government-allied party, the powerful Brazilian Progressive Party.
The PMDB and the PPB are two of the biggest parties in the government's multi-party alliance in Congress and officials Monday began trying to put a damper on Motta's comments.
With PPB leaders expressing outrage, Planning Minister Antonio Kandir told reporters they were "just (Motta's) way of expressing himself."
Motta is regularly in trouble for his unchecked, and often vulgar, criticisms of Brazilian public figures, ranging from the president's wife to leading members of the Catholic Church.

Fortunately for the government, not much of note was likely to happen in Congress until early August when a civil service reform bill and legislation extending the Fiscal Stabilization Fund were due to be put to second full votes in the lower house.

This week, a Senate committee was due to vote on amendments to the government's pension reform bill which it approved last week. Once voting on the amendments is completed, the bill goes to the floor of the Senate for two full votes.
